pl707642.description: Vouni is located on the northwest coast of Cyprus, some 7 km west of Soloi. The rocky hill was occupied in antiquity and the settlement included a fortified palace enclosure, the ancient name of which is unknown. According to PECS, the palace is to be dated ca. 500 to 380 BCE, with two main architectural phases (I: ca. 500 to 450 BCE, II: ca. 450 to 380 BCE).

pl727088.description: Boubastis (also known, in Arabic, as Tell Basta or, in Egyptian, as Per-Bast) was an ancient city in Egypt. It was located in the Nile Delta and served as the capital of the Am-Khent nome (the Bubastite nome), which was the 18th nome of Lower Egypt. It has been identified with the Biblical Pi-Beseth.

pl727097.source: Pleiades (pleiades.stoa.org), Institute for the Study of the Ancient World, CC-BY 3.0
pl727097.description: An ancient Egyptian city of the Nile river delta. Canopus was located in the seventh nome (Menelaites) on the western bank at the mouth of the westernmost branch of the Nile.

pl727169.source: Pleiades (pleiades.stoa.org), Institute for the Study of the Ancient World, CC-BY 3.0
pl727169.description: Naucratis was a city of the Nile river delta, located on the Canopic branch. Capital of Ptolemaic Egypt, Naucratis was the site of permanent Greek habitation from the sixth century BC onward.

pl727217.source: Pleiades (pleiades.stoa.org), Institute for the Study of the Ancient World, CC-BY 3.0
pl727217.description: Sais was an ancient Egyptian town located in the Western Nile Delta on the Canopic branch of the Nile River. It served as the provincial capital of Sap-Meh, the fifth nome of Lower Egypt, and became a capital during the Twenty-fourth Dynasty (ca. 732–720 BC) as well as during the Late Period. Herodotus claimed that Osiris was buried at Sais. Other Greek authors, including Plato, maintained a connection between Sais and the goddess Athena.

pl727227.source: Pleiades (pleiades.stoa.org), Institute for the Study of the Ancient World, CC-BY 3.0
pl727227.description: Sebennytos was an ancient city of Lower Egypt located on the Sebennytic branch of the Nile River. It was the capital of Lower Egypt's twelfth nome (the Sebennyte nome).

pl658378.description: Anazarbos or Anazarbus was an ancient city of Cilicia; its extensive multi-period archaeological remains are located adjacent to the modern village of Dilekkaya in the Kozan district of Turkey's Adana province. pl638783.description: A Roman castellum, located adjacent to the ancient settlement of Aporidos Come and the Aulutrene lake (modern Çapalı/Karakuyu in Turkey's Afyonkarahisar province). An initial (temporary?) camp on/near the location may have been established as early as the second century BC; however, archaeological and epigraphic evidence point to a small, stone-built installation with associated garrison, possibly during the Severan period that was later expanded in Byzantine times. The stone structure, at the modern town of Eldere, was heavily quarried and built over by the 1980s.

pl638837.description: An ancient sanctuary complex, incorporating a cave known today as Zindan Mağarası, which overlooks a bend in the river Aksu (locally Zindan Deresi; a tributary of the Eurymedon) in Turkey's Isparta province. Archaeological and epigraphic evidence demonstrate human activity from the Hellenistic to the Seljuk period, with the dedication of a temple to the Vigenon Mother of the Gods during the reign of Marcus Aurelius. A Roman-era bridge and road section has also been identified as part of the complex, which was probably associated with the nearby city of Timbriada. The sanctuary also honored the god Eurymedon.

There is no evidence for activity at the site in the early Roman empire.

cur-fossil-ubeidiya.dateNote: In 1959 a farmer ploughing south of the Sea of Galilee, Israel, turned up bones and stone tools. Digs led by Moshe Stekelis found hand axes and animal bones about 1.5 million years old: one of the oldest signs of early humans outside Africa.
cur-fossil-ubeidiya.summary: Stone tools 1.5 million years old by the Jordan: early humans outside Africa.

q152378.dateNote: Sources give 1962 or 1963 for his birth.

cur-fossil-hayonim.dateNote: From 1965 Ofer Bar-Yosef and Eitan Tchernov's team dug this cave in western Galilee, Israel. Its layers run from stone tools over 0.2 million years old to Natufian graves about 12,000 years old.
cur-fossil-hayonim.summary: A cave in Galilee with layers from 200,000 years ago up to Natufian graves.

q334821.placeNote: Where he was born is not recorded; the pin is just the middle of Sharqia Governorate.

cur-fossil-kebara.dateNote: In 1983 Ofer Bar-Yosef and Bernard Vandermeersch's team found most of a Neanderthal man's skeleton, nicknamed "Moshe", in this cave on Mount Carmel, Israel. It held the first Neanderthal hyoid (throat) bone ever found. About 60,000 years old (0.06 million years).
cur-fossil-kebara.summary: An Israeli cave where a Neanderthal skeleton kept its throat bone, a clue to how Neanderthals spoke.

cur-fossil-dederiyeh.dateNote: In 1993 a Japanese–Syrian team led by Takeru Akazawa found the skeleton of a Neanderthal child, about two years old, in this cave in north-west Syria. A second child was found in 1997. They are about 50,000 years old (0.05 million years).
cur-fossil-dederiyeh.summary: A Syrian cave where the skeletons of two Neanderthal children were found.

pl48107156.source: Pleiades (pleiades.stoa.org), Institute for the Study of the Ancient World, CC-BY 3.0
pl48107156.description: Tell el-Retaba is a large, multi-phase settlement site located in the central part of Wadi Tumilat. Its human activity ranges from the period of Hyksos settlers to the Third Intermediate Period to the 19th century.

pl276676984.source: Pleiades (pleiades.stoa.org), Institute for the Study of the Ancient World, CC-BY 3.0
pl276676984.description: The monumental sanctuary of Zeus Olympius at Jerash dates to the 160s CE.

pl959992687.source: Pleiades (pleiades.stoa.org), Institute for the Study of the Ancient World, CC-BY 3.0

pl305820069.source: Pleiades (pleiades.stoa.org), Institute for the Study of the Ancient World, CC-BY 3.0
pl305820069.description: A modern village in the Refahiye region of Turkey's Erzincan province where remains of ancient roads and routes converge and where a Roman milestone has been found. In Roman times, it was likely a walled town or fort, garrisoned at some point by the cohors I Lepidiana. Scholarly opinions differ as to its possible names in antiquity.

pl687315572.source: Pleiades (pleiades.stoa.org), Institute for the Study of the Ancient World, CC-BY 3.0
pl687315572.description: A Bronze Age settlement mound, submerged since 1974 in Lake Assad.

pl172140914.source: Pleiades (pleiades.stoa.org), Institute for the Study of the Ancient World, CC-BY 3.0
pl172140914.description: Apliki in central Cyprus was the site of Bronze Age copper smelting.

pl389026185.source: Pleiades (pleiades.stoa.org), Institute for the Study of the Ancient World, CC-BY 3.0
pl389026185.description: Place in Chalcidice in northern Syria, on the road from Chalkis to Ephiphania, mentioned in the Antonine Itinerary.

pl802044826.source: Pleiades (pleiades.stoa.org), Institute for the Study of the Ancient World, CC-BY 3.0
pl802044826.description: A public bath complex built at Palmyra toward the end of the second century CE and perhaps renovated during the reign of Diocletian.

pl774381973.source: Pleiades (pleiades.stoa.org), Institute for the Study of the Ancient World, CC-BY 3.0
pl774381973.description: A copper-smelting slag heap located in the village of Pelathousa in western Cyprus, dating to the 4th-6th century CE and likely derived from ore mined at the Limni mine, which is approximately 1 kilometer to the northwest.

pl774381974.source: Pleiades (pleiades.stoa.org), Institute for the Study of the Ancient World, CC-BY 3.0
pl774381974.description: A copper-smelting slag heap located in the village of Argaka in western Cyprus (Paphos district), dating between the third and eighth centuries CE and likely derived from ore mined at Limni.

pl106515914.source: Pleiades (pleiades.stoa.org), Institute for the Study of the Ancient World, CC-BY 3.0
pl106515914.description: The findspot of a stele from the reign of Nabonidus, the last king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire.

pl989927858.source: Pleiades (pleiades.stoa.org), Institute for the Study of the Ancient World, CC-BY 3.0
pl989927858.description: A low mound on the east bank of the Euphrates, close to the border between Syria and Turkey. Salvage excavations were undertaken here around the year 2000. The site has yielded cuneiform finds.

pl485747633.source: Pleiades (pleiades.stoa.org), Institute for the Study of the Ancient World, CC-BY 3.0
pl485747633.description: An extensive ancient site in northwest Cyprus occupied from the Bronze Age until approximately 700 B.C.

cur-fossil-qesem.dateNote: Found in 2000 during road building near Rosh HaAyin, Israel; digs led by Avi Gopher and Ran Barkai began in 2001. It holds human teeth, hearths and tools from about 400,000–200,000 years ago (0.4–0.2 million years). Wikidata pins the cave at a rounded point.
cur-fossil-qesem.summary: An Israeli cave where people used fire and shared out meat 400,000 years ago.

cur-fossil-misliya.dateNote: In 2002 an upper jaw with teeth was found in Misliya Cave on Mount Carmel, Israel. Israel Hershkovitz's team published it in 2018: Homo sapiens, about 177,000–194,000 years old (0.18 million years), then the oldest found outside Africa.
cur-fossil-misliya.summary: A jaw from Mount Carmel, among the oldest Homo sapiens fossils outside Africa.

cur-fossil-gesher-benot-yaaqov.dateNote: In 2004 Naama Goren-Inbar's team reported burnt seeds, wood and flint at this old lake shore by the River Jordan in northern Israel. They are about 790,000 years old (0.79 million years).
cur-fossil-gesher-benot-yaaqov.summary: A site by the River Jordan with one of the oldest signs of people using fire.

cur-fossil-nesher-ramla.dateNote: In 2021 Israel Hershkovitz and Yossi Zaidner's teams described a skull piece and a jaw from Nesher Ramla, a dig in a quarry near Ramla, Israel. About 140,000–120,000 years old (0.14–0.12 million years), they mix Neanderthal and older features. Pinned at the Wikidata point for the site, Nesher Ramla (Q107314382).
cur-fossil-nesher-ramla.summary: A quarry near Ramla with bones of an unusual early human group, about 130,000 years old.
